Back ends in practice

Stop 2.3 showed what an API is. This is what a back-end developer actually builds all day: routes, rules and the guard rails that keep bad input and double payments out. Twelve words and you can review a back-end plan.

You want toHTTP methodDatabase (SQL)Example route
CreatePOSTINSERTPOST /appointments
ReadGETSELECTGET /appointments?date=2026-10-12
UpdatePUT or PATCHUPDATEPATCH /appointments/42
DeleteDELETEDELETEDELETE /appointments/42
Runtime

The engine that runs back-end code: Node.js, Bun or Deno for JavaScript, Python with FastAPI or Django, PHP, Java's JVM, Go.

Routing

Matching a URL and method to the code that handles it: GET /patients/42 goes to the "show patient" handler.

Middleware

Code that runs on every request before the handler: check the login, check the role, log it, rate-limit it.

API design + contract

Resources as nouns (/patients/42/appointments), methods as verbs, consistent errors. The contract is the promise of what each endpoint takes and returns. OpenAPI writes it as a file that generates docs and SDKs. Internal services sometimes use gRPC, a faster binary alternative to JSON.

Versioning

/v1/ and /v2/ let you change an API without breaking the mobile app people haven't updated.

Pagination, filtering, sorting

Never return 50,000 rows. Return pages (?page=2, or a cursor), with filters (?status=booked) and sorting (?sort=-date).

Idempotency

Doing something twice has the same effect as once. Payment APIs take an Idempotency-Key so a retried request can't charge twice.

Rate limiting

Capping requests per user or IP, answered with status 429. Protects login forms from password guessing and your AI bill from runaway bots.

Input validation + output encoding

Check every incoming field against a schema (Zod in JavaScript, Pydantic in Python). Encode everything you output so user text can't become code (Stop 4.20).

Error handling

One consistent error shape, a useful message for the user, details only in the logs. Never show a stack trace to visitors.

API observability

Logs, response times and error rates per endpoint, so you know which route is slow before the client does.

"Is validation on the server, is the payment endpoint idempotent, and is login rate-limited?" Three questions that catch most back-end corner-cutting.

Try it · 5 min

Open jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts?_limit=3 in your browser: that's a public test API returning JSON, with pagination in the query. Then try /posts/1 and /posts/1/comments, and you're reading REST routes.

Stop 4.14 5 min

Real-time, background jobs and integrations

Some work can't happen while the visitor waits: sending 500 reminders, transcribing a call, syncing with a CRM. And some has to happen instantly: a chat message, an AI voice reply. This stop covers both ends, plus the glue between systems.

Polling

The browser asks "anything new?" every few seconds. Simple, wasteful, fine for a payment status page.

Webhooks

One server calls another when something happens: Razorpay tells your server "payment captured". Always verify the signature and answer quickly.

Server-sent events (SSE)

The server streams updates to the browser over one open connection, one way only. It's how chatbots appear to type word by word.

WebSockets

A two-way connection kept open: chat, live dashboards, multiplayer, audio streams. The concept is simple. Keeping 100,000 of them alive is the hard part.

WebRTC

Peer-to-peer audio, video and data in the browser, built for low latency: video calls and voice AI.

Background jobs + queues

Slow work goes on a queue and workers process it outside the request: BullMQ on Redis, Amazon SQS, Celery, or hosted tools like Inngest and Trigger.dev. Failed jobs retry with backoff, then land in a dead-letter queue for a human.

Cron

Scheduled jobs: "every day at 9 am, send tomorrow's reminders." Named after the Unix scheduler.

Event-driven architecture

Services announce events (appointment.booked) and anyone interested reacts: send a WhatsApp, update the CRM, notify the dentist. Adding a reaction doesn't touch the booking code.

Notification channels

Email (Stop 4.2), push (Stop 4.5), SMS (in India commercial SMS needs TRAI DLT registration of your sender ID and templates), and WhatsApp.

WhatsApp Business Platform

Through Meta's Cloud API or a provider like Gupshup, Interakt, AiSensy or Twilio. Business-started messages need pre-approved templates, and replies are tied to a 24-hour customer service window. Meta charges per template message since July 2025, and from 1 October 2026 also for service replies inside the window.

Integrations

n8n, Zapier and Make connect apps through their APIs and webhooks. n8n can be self-hosted, which matters when the data is medical.

Reprice your WhatsApp automations this week. Meta's per-message charge on service replies started 1 October 2026. Anything you quoted as "replies are free" needs a fresh cost line, ideally passed through at cost plus margin.

"What happens when this job fails at 3 am: does it retry, and who finds out?"

Try it · 5 min

Open webhook.site to get a free test URL. In n8n, add an HTTP Request node that POSTs a small JSON message to it, run it, and watch the webhook arrive live. That's the whole idea behind every integration.

Stop 4.15 5 min

Serverless, edge and the cloud contract

"Serverless" doesn't mean no servers. It means they're someone else's problem: you upload functions, the provider runs them only when called, and you pay per use. It's brilliant for spiky, small workloads and a trap for the wrong ones.

Service models

IaaS: rent virtual machines (EC2, DigitalOcean). PaaS: push code and it runs (Render, Railway, Heroku). FaaS / serverless: upload functions (AWS Lambda since 2014, Vercel and Netlify Functions, Cloudflare Workers). BaaS: login, database and storage ready-made (Supabase, Firebase).

Scales to zero

No traffic, no bill. Spikes scale automatically. Perfect for a clinic site's contact form and webhooks.

Cold start

The pause when a function hasn't run for a while and has to boot. Usually milliseconds to a second, noticeable on voice and chat.

Limits

Functions are stateless and time-limited (Lambda's maximum is 15 minutes), and are bad at long-lived connections like WebSockets. Long jobs belong on a queue with a worker or a container.

Edge

Code that runs in data centres close to the visitor (Cloudflare Workers, Vercel Edge): redirects, A/B splits, geo rules, auth checks in milliseconds.

Regions + availability zones

A region is a geographic area (AWS Mumbai is ap-south-1); availability zones are separate data centres inside it. Pick the region for latency and for where health data should live.

Autoscaling

Adding and removing capacity automatically as load changes. Set a maximum, or a bot attack becomes a bill.

Infrastructure as code

Servers, databases and DNS described in files (Terraform or OpenTofu, Pulumi) and versioned in Git, so environments can be rebuilt identically.

Twelve-Factor + environment parity

A 2011 checklist for cloud-ready apps: config in environment variables, stateless processes, logs as streams, and dev, staging and production kept as alike as possible.

Well-Architected

AWS's six pillars for reviewing any system: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimisation, sustainability.

Cost management

Budgets and alerts, tagging resources per client, and watching data transfer (egress) fees. "Denial of wallet" is when an attack makes you pay instead of taking you down.

Vendor lock-in

The more provider-specific services you use, the harder it is to move. It's a trade, not a sin: write down what you're locked into and why.

Plate 13 · Cloud

Serverless

Rents a shell only when it needs one · AWS Lambda arrived in 2014

  • Field marksCode as small functions, triggered by an HTTP request, a schedule or an event, billed per request and per millisecond.
  • Habitat/api routes on Vercel and Netlify, Cloudflare Workers, Lambda behind API Gateway, Supabase Edge Functions.
  • You'll hear"Cold start", "scales to zero", "edge function", "it timed out", "pay per invocation".
  • Confused with"No servers". There are servers; you just never see, patch or pay for them while idle.
Social proof
Most modern agency stacks (Next.js on Vercel plus Supabase) are serverless by default.
For you
A clinic site on serverless often costs nothing to host at its traffic, so sell the care and the features, not the hosting.

"Does it scale to zero, and what does the bill look like at ten times today's traffic?"

"Which parts are serverless, which need a long-running worker, and where does the patient data live?"

Try it · 5 min

Open the usage or billing page of any cloud you use (Vercel, Supabase, AWS, Google Cloud) and set a budget alert, even a $5 one. It's the single most protective click in cloud computing.

Stop 4.16 4 min

Data in practice

Stop 2.4 introduced the database species. This is how they're actually used: how data gets shaped, kept fast, changed safely and brought back after a disaster. Most expensive production incidents start here.

Data modelling

Deciding the tables (or collections), their fields and how they relate, before writing code. A primary key identifies each row; a foreign key points to a row in another table.

Indexes

Like a book's index: lookups by phone number go from scanning a million rows to a few steps. Each index speeds up reads and slightly slows writes.

Joins

Combining rows from related tables in one query: appointments with their patient names and dentist names.

Transactions (ACID)

A group of changes that all happen or none do: book the slot and record the deposit, or neither. Atomic, consistent, isolated, durable.

Migrations

Versioned scripts that change the database structure, stored in Git and run the same way everywhere. Nobody edits the production database by hand.

Connection pooling

Databases accept a limited number of connections, and serverless functions open lots. A pooler (PgBouncer, Supabase's Supavisor, Neon's built-in pooling) shares them.

Caching strategy

Keep popular answers in Redis or a CDN, and decide how they expire or get invalidated. "There are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things."

Replication

Copies of the database on other machines: read replicas share the load, and a standby takes over if the primary fails. With automatic failover, that's high availability: no single machine whose death takes the app down.

Backups + restore

The 3-2-1 rule: three copies, on two kinds of storage, one off-site. A backup you've never restored is a hope, not a backup. Point-in-time recovery lets you rewind to any minute.

Disaster recovery

RPO (recovery point objective): how much recent data you can afford to lose. RTO (recovery time objective): how long you can be down. Both are business decisions with prices.

Data pipelines

Moving data from the app into a warehouse (BigQuery, Snowflake) for reporting, with ETL or ELT jobs, so heavy analysis doesn't slow the live app.

"What's our RPO and RTO, and when did we last test a restore?"

Try it · 5 min

Draw the clinic data model on paper: Patient, Dentist, Appointment, Treatment, Invoice. Write "1 to many" or "1 to 1" on every line. If two people would draw it differently, the build will go wrong there.

Stop 4.17 4 min

Payments and money flows

Taking money online looks like one button. Behind it are a gateway, a bank, card or UPI rails, a confirmation message and a dozen ways to get it wrong. Clinics want deposits; your US clients want subscriptions.

Payment gateway

The service that collects payment details and routes them: Razorpay, Cashfree, PayU in India; Stripe, Square and PayPal abroad. Fees are a small percentage per transaction.

Payment methods

Cards, UPI, netbanking, wallets, EMI and pay-later. UPI handled a record 24.5 billion transactions in August 2026, so it's the default for Indian patients.

Payment intent / order

An object that tracks one payment through its states: created, needs authentication (OTP or 3-D Secure), succeeded or failed. You create it on the server, not in the browser.

Webhooks for payments

The gateway calls your server with a signed message when money moves. Verify the signature, handle duplicates, and only then mark the order paid.

Subscriptions + mandates

Recurring billing: a plan, a billing cycle, retries for failed cards. In India recurring payments run on mandates (UPI AutoPay, card e-mandates) under RBI rules, including pre-debit notices.

Refunds + chargebacks

A refund is you returning money. A chargeback is the customer's bank forcibly reversing it after a dispute. Too many and the gateway can freeze the account.

PCI DSS

The card industry's security standard. Use the gateway's hosted checkout or elements so card numbers never touch your server; that keeps your compliance work tiny.

Settlement

Money reaches the merchant's bank a day or two after the payment (T+1, T+2), minus fees. Clients will ask why the dashboard and the bank differ.

Merchant of record

Paddle or Lemon Squeezy sell on your behalf and handle global sales tax: useful for selling software to US and EU buyers from India.

"Do we mark orders paid from the webhook, and is it idempotent?"

Try it · 5 min

Open Razorpay's or Stripe's test mode and make a fake payment with a test card or test UPI ID. Then find the webhook event log in the dashboard and read what it would have sent your server.

Stop 4.18 4 min

Shipping safely: tests and releases

"It works on my machine" is how most bugs are born. Professional teams catch problems with layers of automatic tests and release in stages, so a mistake reaches 5% of users for ten minutes instead of everyone for a weekend.

Unit tests

Check one small piece in isolation: does the fee calculator add GST correctly?

Integration tests

Check pieces working together: does booking actually write to a real test database and queue a reminder?

End-to-end tests

A robot browser (Playwright, Cypress) clicks through the real flow: open site, pick slot, pay, see confirmation.

Load testing

Simulate hundreds or thousands of users (k6, JMeter) before the Diwali campaign, not during it.

Linting + formatting + types

ESLint flags likely bugs, Prettier formats code the same way for everyone, TypeScript catches type mistakes before the code runs.

Branching strategy

Trunk-based (small branches merged daily) or GitFlow (long-lived develop and release branches). Small and frequent wins for small teams. When two branches change the same lines, Git raises a merge conflict that a human resolves.

Semantic versioning

MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: 2.4.1 to 2.4.2 is a fix, to 2.5.0 adds features, to 3.0.0 may break things.

Lockfiles

package-lock.json or poetry.lock pin the exact version of every dependency, so tomorrow's build matches today's.

Build artifact

The finished output you deploy (a bundle, a Docker image), built once and promoted unchanged from staging to production.

Environments

Local, preview (Vercel makes one per pull request), staging and production. Staging should mirror production; Stop 4.15's environment parity.

Canary + rollback

Release to a small slice of users first and watch errors. If they rise, roll back with one click. Blue-green releases switch between two complete copies.

"What would catch it if this dependency update broke checkout tonight?"

Try it · 5 min

Open any project on GitHub and find three things: the lockfile (package-lock.json or similar), the .github/workflows folder (the CI robots), and a tests folder. You'll be able to judge a repo's maturity in under a minute.

Stop 4.19 4 min

Keeping it alive: monitoring and incidents

Launch day is the start, not the end. Live software breaks: a certificate expires, a provider has an outage, a plugin update clashes. Professionals find out before the client does, fix it by playbook, and learn from it in writing.

Uptime targetAllowed downtime per monthRealistic for
99%about 7 hoursA hobby project
99.5%about 3.6 hoursA small business site
99.9%about 43 minutesMost serious web apps
99.99%about 4 minutesPayments, health systems, big budgets
Logs, metrics, traces

Logs: timestamped event lines. Metrics: numbers over time (errors per minute, response time). Traces: one request's journey across every service. OpenTelemetry is the open standard for all three.

Error tracking

Sentry and similar tools group crashes, show the line of code, the browser and the steps leading up to it.

Uptime monitoring

A robot checks the site every minute from several countries and alerts you when it fails: Better Stack, UptimeRobot.

Alerting

Wake a human only for things users feel. Too many alerts and people learn to ignore all of them.

SLI, SLO, SLA

SLI: what you measure (requests answered under 500 ms). SLO: your target (99.9%). SLA: the contract with penalties if you miss it. Promise SLAs below your SLOs.

Error budget

The 0.1% you're allowed to fail. Spend it on shipping features; when it's gone, slow down and fix reliability.

Incident response

Detect, triage, mitigate (roll back first, investigate later), communicate (a status page, a message to the client), resolve.

Runbooks

Step-by-step playbooks for known problems: "site down", "emails bouncing", "database full". Written while calm, used while panicking.

Postmortems

A blameless write-up after an incident: what happened, why, what we change. Clients trust an agency that sends one.

This stop is your retainer, itemised: uptime monitoring, error tracking, backups with a tested restore, security and plugin updates, a monthly one-page report. That's what $300-500 a month buys, and it's easy to justify when it's listed.

"How would we know the site was down at 2 am, and who gets the alert?"

Try it · 5 min

Create a free uptime monitor for one live client site (Better Stack or UptimeRobot) with alerts to your phone. Then write a five-line runbook for "the site is down": who checks what, in which order.

Stop 4.20 5 min

Security, the OWASP 2025 way

Stop 2.11 covered security basics and compliance. This is the industry's own list of how web apps actually get broken into, as updated in 2025, with the one-line fix for each. Health portals make you a target, so learn these names.

#Risk (OWASP Top 10:2025)What it looks likeThe fix
A01Broken access controlChange the ID in the URL, see someone else's X-rays. Also covers SSRF and CSRF nowCheck permissions on the server for every record, deny by default
A02Security misconfigurationDebug mode on, default passwords, a public storage bucketHardened configs, reviewed on every deploy
A03Software supply chain failuresA malicious or hijacked npm package in your buildLockfiles, fewer dependencies, Dependabot or Renovate, trusted sources
A04Cryptographic failuresNo HTTPS, passwords stored with weak hashingTLS everywhere, bcrypt or Argon2, encryption at rest
A05InjectionSQL injection; XSS (cross-site scripting), where user text runs as code in other people's browsersParameterised queries, output encoding, a Content Security Policy
A06Insecure designA reset flow anyone can abuse, no matter how well codedThreat modelling before building
A07Authentication failuresUnlimited password guesses, no 2FA, sessions that never expireRate limits, MFA or passkeys, short sessions
A08Software or data integrity failuresUnsigned updates, a tampered CI pipelineSigned artifacts, protected pipelines
A09Security logging and alerting failuresA breach nobody notices for monthsLog security events and alert on them
A10Mishandling of exceptional conditionsErrors that leak details, or fail open and grant accessFail safely, show generic errors, log the details
XSS

Cross-site scripting: an attacker gets their script into a page others view (a review, a name field) and it runs as them. Frameworks escape output by default; don't switch that off.

SSRF

Server-side request forgery: tricking your server into fetching internal addresses, like cloud metadata that holds secret keys. Matters for AI tools that fetch URLs.

Content Security Policy

An HTTP header listing which scripts and sources a page may load. Turns many XSS attacks into harmless errors.

Secrets management

Keys live in environment variables or a vault (Doppler, AWS Secrets Manager, 1Password), are rotated, and never sit in Git or chat.

Encryption in transit + at rest

TLS on every connection; encrypted disks and backups. Health data gets both, plus access logs.

Vulnerability management

Track known holes (CVEs) in what you run, patch on a schedule, and have a deadline for critical fixes.

Threat modelling

Before building, ask what could go wrong: STRIDE lists spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege.

Secure SDLC

Security at every step of building software: design review, code review, dependency scans, tests, monitoring. Not a pen test the week before launch.

"Which of the OWASP Top 10 did you test for, and how?" Any security vendor worth paying answers that specifically.

Try it · 5 min

Run one of your live sites through securityheaders.com. Note which headers are missing (Content-Security-Policy, Strict-Transport-Security, X-Content-Type-Options) and ask your developer to add them. It takes an hour and impresses every auditor.

Stop 4.21 4 min

Product, design and UX

You position MTRX as a design studio, so this is your home turf, in the words product teams use. The order matters: every step you skip on the way to a pretty mockup comes back later as a rework invoice.

Product requirements (PRD)

One document: the problem, who has it, goals, what's in and out of scope, and how success is measured.

User stories

"As a patient, I want to reschedule online, so I don't have to call during work hours." Small, user-shaped pieces of work.

Acceptance criteria

When a story counts as done: "Given a booked appointment, when I pick a new slot, then the old one is released and I get a WhatsApp confirmation." A team-wide definition of done adds the standing rules: tested, reviewed, accessible, deployed.

Information architecture

How content is organised and labelled: the sitemap, the navigation, what each page is called. Card sorting with real users settles arguments.

User journey

Every step a person takes, online and off, from "my tooth hurts" to "booked" to "reminder" to "review". Find the drop-off points.

Wireframe, mockup, prototype

Wireframe: layout in grey boxes. Mockup: the real visual design. Prototype: clickable screens in Figma that feel like the product.

Design system

Reusable rules and parts: colour, type and spacing tokens, plus components like buttons, inputs and cards (shadcn/ui, Material). One source of truth for designers and developers.

UX and usability

How easy and pleasant it is to get things done. Nielsen's 10 heuristics are the classic checklist. Watching five users try the real task finds most big problems.

Conversion funnel + CRO

The steps from visit to booking, and conversion rate optimisation: improving the step where most people drop.

Empty, loading and error states

What the screen shows with no data yet, while waiting, and when something fails. Skeleton screens and helpful errors make products feel finished.

Responsive interaction

Tap targets big enough for thumbs, no hover-only menus, forms that work one-handed on a phone.

"What's the one task this page must make easy, and how will we know it worked?"

Try it · 5 min

Write three user stories with acceptance criteria for a patient portal: view X-rays, reschedule, download an invoice. Then watch one non-technical person try your live site's booking flow without help, and note where they hesitate.

Stop 4.22 4 min

How software projects actually run

Most failed software projects don't fail on code. They fail on scope, estimates, handovers and contracts. This is the operating manual of a delivery team, and the clauses that keep an agency profitable.

Pricing modelHow it worksRisk sits withGood for
Fixed priceOne price for an agreed scopeYouClear brochure sites, well-defined builds
Time and materialsHours or days at a rateThe clientFuzzy or evolving products
RetainerMonthly fee for a bucket of work or careSharedMaintenance, SEO, ongoing improvements
MilestonesPayments tied to delivered stagesSharedMost agency projects, as a hybrid
Agile

A 2001 manifesto: deliver working software in small increments and adapt to feedback. A mindset more than a method.

Scrum

Fixed sprints of one to four weeks, with planning, a daily stand-up, a review demo and a retrospective. The most common way teams practise agile.

Kanban

A board of cards moving across columns, with limits on work in progress. Great for maintenance and support work.

Shape Up

Basecamp's method: shape the work properly, then a fixed six-week cycle with a fixed team and a flexible scope.

Backlog + prioritisation

The ordered list of everything not yet done. MoSCoW (must, should, could, won't) is the quickest way to sort it with a client.

Retrospective

After each sprint or project: what went well, what didn't, what we change. The cheapest improvement habit in software.

Estimation

Hours, days or relative story points. Early estimates are guesses: the classic "cone of uncertainty" says they can be off by up to four times either way, narrowing as you learn.

Scope management

Writing down what's in, what's out, and how changes are requested and priced. Scope creep is unpriced change.

Risk register

A short list of what could go wrong, how likely, how bad, and the plan. Clients love seeing one; it signals seniority.

Technical debt

Shortcuts taken now that cost interest later (Ward Cunningham's 1992 metaphor). Some debt is smart, if you write it down and pay it back.

Documentation

A README for setup, decision records explaining why things were built a certain way, runbooks for operations. The handover is mostly documentation.

Open-source licences

MIT and Apache: use freely, keep the notice. GPL: if you distribute changes, you share the source. AGPL: even running it as a web service can trigger that. Check before you build a client's product on it.

Terms and IP

Terms of service and a privacy policy for the product; in your contract, intellectual property passes to the client on final payment, and you keep the right to reuse your own generic code.

Add three clauses to every MTRX proposal: a change-request process with a day rate, payment milestones, and a handover checklist (repository, domain and DNS access, hosting, admin logins, documentation). They prevent most agency fights before they start.

"What's out of scope, and how do we handle change requests?" Ask it at kickoff, in writing.

Try it · 5 min

Build a reusable client project template in ClickUp: Discovery, Design, Build, QA, Launch, Handover, with the handover checklist as subtasks. Use it on the next dental client.

Stop 4.23 5 min

The CS degree in one stop

A four-year computer science degree (the ACM and IEEE CS2023 curriculum) has 17 knowledge areas. Most of it trains people to build systems from scratch. You need some of it in depth and the rest as mental models, so you can follow an engineer's reasoning without doing their maths.

Bits, bytes and memory

Everything is binary. A byte is 8 bits, text is bytes, images are many bytes. The CPU computes, RAM holds what's in use, disks hold what's stored.

Latency ladder

Rough orders of magnitude: CPU cache in nanoseconds, RAM about 100 ns, an SSD read around 100 microseconds, a same-city network call a millisecond or so, another continent 100+ ms. This is why caching works.

Paradigms

Imperative (step-by-step instructions), object-oriented (objects with data and behaviour), functional (pure functions, no hidden changes), declarative (say what you want, like SQL).

Control flow + functions

If-else, loops and functions are the grammar of every language. Modules group functions into reusable files and packages.

Data structures

Array (a numbered list), hash map (instant lookup by key), tree (hierarchy, like folders), graph (networks, like maps or social links), queue and stack (first in first out, last in first out).

Algorithms + Big-O

How work grows with data. O(1): instant. O(log n): binary search, a million items in about 20 steps. O(n): read everything once. O(n²): compare everything with everything, which explodes at scale. The maths underneath (discrete mathematics, logic, probability) your MSc already covers.

Compilers, interpreters, runtimes

Compilers translate code to machine code ahead of time (Rust, Go). Interpreters run it line by line (classic Python). Runtimes and virtual machines like Java's JVM and Chrome's V8 compile on the fly (JIT).

Processes, threads, concurrency

A process is a running program with its own memory; threads are workers inside it. Concurrency is juggling many tasks; parallelism is doing them at the same moment on many cores. Race conditions and deadlocks are what go wrong.

Distributed systems

Many machines acting as one, over unreliable networks. The CAP theorem: when the network splits, you choose between consistency and availability.

Fault tolerance

Designing so one failure isn't total failure: redundancy, retries, timeouts, graceful degradation.

Choosing a language

Pick by ecosystem, hiring pool, the team's skills and the job (Stop 2.9), not by fashion. Boring choices ship.

"What's the Big-O of that, and does it matter at our data size?" Often the honest answer is "not yet", and that's fine.

Try it · 5 min

Watch lecture 0 of Harvard's free CS50 (cs50.harvard.edu): binary, algorithms and the phone-book search that makes O(log n) obvious. It's the best single hour of computer science online.
